misconceptions.description: Believing disclosure of AI use is a rule only students must follow, not teachers
misconceptions.trigger: teacher uses AI to write feedback or recommendation letters without disclosing it
misconceptions.feedback: Transparency runs both ways. If AI substantially shaped feedback, grades, or a recommendation, disclose your use to the affected reader, just as you ask students to disclose theirs.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a blanket label like "AI was used" satisfies meaningful disclosure
misconceptions.trigger: student or teacher tags work "made with AI" without saying what AI did
misconceptions.feedback: Meaningful disclosure states what the AI did, what the human did, and what was verified or rejected. A bare label is not enough for a reader to judge the work.

misconceptions.description: Treating disclosure of allowed AI use as a confession that lowers the grade
misconceptions.trigger: student hides permitted AI assistance because disclosure feels like admitting cheating
misconceptions.feedback: Disclosing allowed use is honesty, not guilt. Make clear that transparent, permitted use is expected and is not penalized, so students do not hide it.

misconceptions.description: Believing that disclosing AI use shifts responsibility for errors onto the tool
misconceptions.trigger: author blames the AI for a mistake because the AI was disclosed
misconceptions.feedback: Disclosure does not transfer accountability. The human who submits the work still owns its accuracy; disclosure informs the reader, it does not excuse errors.
